hook: One LLM call takes 2 seconds. Fifty in a row take 100. Fifty **concurrently** take 4. asyncio is the single highest-leverage Python skill for GenAI apps.

scenes.title: Same idea as C# — **different runtime**
scenes.sub: Coroutines: functions that can pause and resume

steps.at: doesn't RUN when you call it

scenes.narration: If you know C-sharp's async and await, the syntax will feel like home — but Python's runtime works differently underneath. An async def function doesn't RUN when you call it; it returns a coroutine — a paused function object waiting to be executed. Awaiting it hands control back to the event loop, which runs other coroutines while this one waits on I/O. The payoff in GenAI: LLM calls, embedding calls, database queries are all I-O — the CPU sits idle nearly all the time. Concurrency without threads, processes, or locks — one thread juggling thousands of in-flight network calls.

scenes.title: async def doesn't run — it returns a coroutine
scenes.body:
import asyncio

async def summarize(doc: str) -> str:
    resp = await client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize: {doc}"}],
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.content

coro = summarize("quarterly_report.pdf")
print(coro)          # <coroutine object …> — NOT a summary!

# To actually run it, you need an event loop:
summary = asyncio.run(summarize("quarterly_report.pdf"))

# Inside async code, you await instead:
async def main():
    summary = await summarize("quarterly_report.pdf")
    print(summary)
annot: Calling an async function returns a coroutine object — the classic silent bug is forgetting await
await is the pause point: the loop runs other coroutines while this one waits on the network
asyncio.run() creates the loop — call it exactly once, at the top level of your program
scenes.narration: The mental model in one slide. Calling an async function returns a coroutine object — nothing has run yet. Awaiting it tells the event loop: run this, and while it waits on the network, run something else. Asyncio-dot-run creates the event loop and drives everything to completion — it's the entry point you call once, typically under if name equals main. The classic beginner bug: calling an async function, getting a coroutine object back, and printing it wondering where the answer is. If a function is async, SOMEONE must await it, all the way up the call chain to the event loop.

scenes.title: One thread, a to-do list, and **zero idle waiting**
scenes.sub: How Python schedules thousands of coroutines

lines: net done → A is ready again

actors.t: a coroutine that never awaits starves all

steps.at: The event loop is a single thread
then switches to the next ready

scenes.narration: The event loop is a single thread running one loop: it keeps a queue of coroutines that are READY to run, picks one, runs it until it hits an await — a pause point — then switches to the next ready coroutine. Crucially, when a coroutine awaits a network response, the loop doesn't sit there; it runs OTHER work, and a completion notification re-queues the paused coroutine when its I-O finishes. That's why one thread handles thousands of concurrent connections: the CPU is never the bottleneck in I-O-bound work — waiting is. Asyncio converts waiting into doing. It's cooperative multitasking: coroutines yield control at awaits, so a coroutine that never awaits starves everything else.

do: one CPU task blocks the whole loop

scenes.narration: Compare with threads: the OS switches threads preemptively, mid-instruction, so shared data needs locks. Coroutines switch only at awaits — points where YOU know it's safe — so within one event loop, shared state needs no locks at all. The trade: anything CPU-heavy inside a coroutine blocks the entire loop, because nothing else can run until it awaits. Rule: async for waiting on the network, threads or processes for CPU work — PY-11 goes deep on that split. And a sharp edge for GenAI apps: some libraries are secretly blocking — a sync SDK call inside an async function freezes the whole loop; use async-native clients like httpx.

scenes.title: gather: your calls run **in parallel**, your code stays linear
scenes.narration: Gather takes a list of coroutines and runs them all concurrently, returning results in order — it doesn't matter which finishes first. Fifty summarize calls in gather complete in roughly the time of the slowest single call, not fifty times that. But uncapped concurrency is how you rate-limit yourself into a 429 error: fifty simultaneous requests may exceed the API's limits. The Semaphore is the dial: it allows at most N coroutines into a region at once — acquire a slot, do the work, release. Ten LLM calls at a time is a polite, fast, limit-respecting default. Gather for parallelism, semaphore for politeness.

scenes.title: gather + Semaphore: fast AND polite
scenes.body:
import asyncio

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)   # max 10 in-flight API calls

async def summarize(doc: str) -> str:
    async with sem:            # acquire a slot (wait if all 10 taken)
        resp = await client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize: {doc}"}],
        )
        return resp.choices[0].message.content

async def main(docs: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    # all coroutines run CONCURRENTLY; sem caps in-flight at 10
    return await asyncio.gather(*[summarize(d) for d in docs])

# 50 docs × ~2s each:
#   sequential: ~100s     gather without sem: fast but 429s
#   gather + semaphore(10): ~10-12s, limit-friendly
summaries = asyncio.run(main(docs))
annot: Results come back IN ORDER from gather — positional mapping, regardless of finish order
The semaphore lives inside summarize, not main — every call passes through the same gate
exceptions: one failing coroutine fails the whole gather — wrap with return_exceptions=True to tolerate
scenes.narration: This is the production pattern for batch LLM work — embedding a folder of documents, summarizing a backlog, evaluating a golden set. Three subtleties. First, gather preserves order: results align with inputs positionally, even though completion order is random — no manual matching. Second, the semaphore belongs INSIDE the worker function, so every code path through it shares one gate — semaphores scattered at call sites leak concurrency. Third, failure handling: by default one exception fails everything; for batch jobs you usually want return-exceptions equals True, so one bad document doesn't kill forty-nine good summaries. You'll see this exact pattern again in the Agentic stages — agent tools batch the same way.

scenes.title: Networks hang. **Your code must not.**

steps.at: wraps a coroutine with a deadline
give the WHOLE gather a budget
it's the difference between a demo

scenes.narration: Without timeouts, one hung API call stalls a gather forever — your batch job dies of old age at ninety-nine percent complete. asyncio.wait-for wraps a coroutine with a deadline: exceed it, and the coroutine is CANCELLED — a CancelledError raised at its current await. Cancellation is cooperative: the coroutine should clean up at the await point — closing connections, releasing semaphores happen automatically with async-with. Layered strategy for API calls: a per-request timeout slightly above the API's own, retry transient failures with exponential backoff, and give the WHOLE gather a budget so fifty retries can't stretch your job to infinity. Reliability isn't a feature; it's the difference between a demo and a pipeline.

actors.t: speed is worthless if worst case = forever

scenes.narration: The three-layer reliability stack. Timeouts make single calls bounded — without them, tail latency becomes infinite latency. Retry with exponential backoff handles the API's bad days: rate limits and server errors are transient, so wait — one second, two, four — and try again; but distinguish 4-x-x client errors, which retrying cannot fix. And budget the aggregate: per-call timeouts times retry counts can still sum into a hung job, so cap the whole gather. Note httpx has built-in timeout and retry-friendly behavior — PY-12 covers it — so much of this comes free with the right client. Asynchronous code's speed is worthless if its worst case is forever.

quiz.q: What does calling an async function (without await) actually return?
opts: A coroutine object that hasn't started running — it must be awaited (or passed to the loop) to execute
quiz.why: The coroutine is a paused computation; awaiting hands it to the event loop, which runs it to its first I/O pause.

quiz.q: Why pair asyncio.gather with a Semaphore for LLM API calls?
opts: Semaphores make gather return ordered results
Gather maximizes concurrency, which can exceed API rate limits — the semaphore caps in-flight requests
quiz.why: Concurrency without a cap invites 429 rate-limit errors; a semaphore of ~10 is fast yet polite.

quiz.q: What happens when asyncio.wait_for's deadline expires?
opts: The coroutine is cancelled — CancelledError is raised at its current await point
quiz.why: Cancellation is cooperative: it lands at an await, where async-with blocks release resources cleanly.

code.title: Production batch pattern: gather + semaphore + timeout + retry
annot: Timeout INSIDE the retry loop: each attempt gets its own 30s, not the whole retry chain
return_exceptions=True converts failures into values in-place — the batch always completes
Outer wait_for budgets the entire run: bounded worst case regardless of retry storms

notes:
# asyncio

## async / await
- `async def` → calling returns a **coroutine object**; nothing runs until awaited.
- `asyncio.run(main())` — entry point, called once.
- Mental model: C# syntax, single-threaded cooperative runtime.

## Event loop
- One thread; queue of ready coroutines; runs each to its next `await`.
- While a coroutine waits on I/O, others run — waiting becomes doing.
- CPU-heavy work inside a coroutine blocks the whole loop (→ PY-11).
- Beware sync/blocking calls inside async code — freezes the loop; use httpx (PY-12).

## gather & Semaphore
- `asyncio.gather(*coros)` — concurrent execution, **ordered results**.
- `Semaphore(N)` caps in-flight calls — rate-limit politeness.
- `return_exceptions=True` — batch survives individual failures.

## Timeouts & cancellation
- `asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout)` → CancelledError at the await point.
- Retry transient (429/5xx) with exponential backoff; fail fast on 4xx.
- Budget the whole batch — per-call timeouts × retries ≠ bounded runtime.
